author: TEDx Talks
description:
In early morning bicycle rides through London, filmmaker Johno Verity discovers that learning your city's hidden history transforms how you see it, and how you see yourself.  Johno Verity is a London-based content creator, filmmaker, and urban historian known for uncovering and sharing the hidden history of cities through cycling and storytelling. Often described as “London’s cycling historian,” he explores London in the early hours of the morning, revealing the social, architectural, and historical stories embedded in familiar streets, bridges, and public spaces. 

Through short-form videos and visual storytelling, Johno has built a large and engaged audience by making history accessible, informal, and deeply connected to everyday life. His work has been featured by Cycling Weekly and the BBC, where he has been recognized for presenting history in a way that is both engaging and relatable. 

Before turning his focus to urban history, Johno worked as a professional skier and filmmaker
title: Struggling to love your city? Learn its secrets | Johno Verity | TEDxLondonBusinessSchool

Through compelling storytelling and a live demonstration, James explores a transformative truth: painful circumstances can produce powerful outcomes—and our greatest success may ultimately be measured not by what we achieve, but by how we serve others. Best known for martial arts action, the 4x ISKA World Champion in self-defense has appeared in numerous films as an actor, stuntman, fight choreographer, and weapons consultant, including Lethal Weapon 4, Blade, and Netflix’s #1 Plane, which starred Gerard Butler.

Breaking the mold of traditional talks, Lynn Pietig demonstrates the power of persistence in real-time by pulling three live deadlifts on stage, culminating in a historic lift 1 pound above the current world record – creating the first-ever “TEDx Fargo Unofficial World Record.”

Lynn Pietig is a world-class masters powerlifter who proves that it is never too late to chase your ultimate passion and redefine what is possible at any stage of life.

Key Takeaways:
  *Why saying “yes” to small steps unlocks extraordinary outcomes.
  *How to apply the discipline of elite training to any personal passion.
  *Proof that age is just a number when chasing your biggest goals.

description: Ron Ness will provide an overview of North Dakota’s energy potential and technological future, particularly focusing on enhanced oil recovery (EOR) and natural gas infrastructure. There is immense opportunity in the Bakken region, estimating 3 to 7 billion barrels of additional oil recoverable through advanced EOR methods, with another 1 billion barrels possible from conventional oil fields. However, produced gas alone cannot meet future EOR demands, emphasizing the importance of utilizing CO₂ from North Dakota’s industrial sources to achieve the full recovery potential. There are planned EOR projects scheduled in North Dakota, such as multi-well and multi-zone pilots in Williams and Dunn Counties, as well as surfactant-based EOR tests. These efforts reflect a transition toward a zero-emission, technology-driven Bakken, featuring advancements like four-mile laterals, U-turn drilling, and improved wellsite efficiency and gas capture systems. From testifying before Philadelphia City Council to publishing in The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times, her work is helping shape conversations that directly impact the safety and well-being of children nationwide. description:
How do we find hope when life brings us the unthinkable—something we cannot control, change, or fix? 

We may try to muscle through grief, anxiety, trauma, or heartbreak, but difficult emotions don't disappear. They often surface as anxiety, numbness, avoidance, low motivation, or the need to control. When we shut out pain, we often lose the ability to feel joy.

Katie Kelley Dorn learned this through her work as a licensed therapist and school counselor—but most profoundly as a mother of seven. Drawing on the loss of her beloved sister Ginny, welcoming Ginny's three children into her family, and helping thousands of students and families, Katie shares what she discovered when powering through—and trying to fix everything—stopped working.

description:
Twenty-five years ago, technology was one of the greatest limits for artists. A VFX product could take months to complete, requiring an entire team and complex tools. Today, as AI can generate images within minutes, many technological limits seem to have been removed. The question is no longer what the tools can do, but how far human imagination can go.
Mr. Thierry Nguyen showed that technological limits can sometimes be what force artists to build a stronger creative foundation. Before AI, artists did not have predictive models or massive databases to create images for them. They had to learn how to observe, understand movement, feel the visuals, and tell stories through every frame. Those limits made the creative process slower, but they also pushed people to understand what they were creating and why it mattered.

Rather than allowing that judgment to define her, she saw it as a starting point to pursue bigger opportunities and challenge the limits placed on her.

As we step further beyond our comfort zones, rejection, judgment, and failure can easily make us question ourselves. Mook emphasized that overcoming these moments requires more than confidence—it requires Internal Authority, the ability to believe that we belong where we are heading before receiving external validation. Breaking boundaries begins when we stop accepting “enough” as our limit and take back the power to define how far we can go. Mook Karnruethai Tassabut’s journey brings this idea to life. What if becoming a better leader starts with learning how to regulate yourself?

Alicia Dugar Stephenson shares a deeply personal journey through difficult relationships, chronic illness, and a constant state of survival—and how those experiences transformed the way she understands leadership.

After recognizing patterns in her own life and being diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus while at university, Alicia began to see how living in a heightened state of survival could affect the way she responded to the world around her.

Her turning point came through yoga.

Not simply as exercise, but as a practice of self-regulation: learning to notice tension, fear, and physical reactions before allowing them to determine her response.

Alicia argues that self-regulation is one of the most overlooked leadership skills. When pressure rises, the ability to pause rather than react can change the quality of our decisions, our relationships, and the environment we create for the people arou

Why do we feel more disconnected even when we're constantly surrounded by people?

Carlos Hernandez explores the growing loneliness crisis and argues that the problem may go deeper than smartphones, screens, or social media. In his view, technology isn't the wound—it's the bandage. The deeper issue is our growing intention deficit: showing up physically without deciding how we want to truly be present.

Carlos shares lessons from founding the mood room, an intentional social space in Houston, where he noticed something surprising: people who arrived with a clear purpose connected more deeply and more quickly than those who simply showed up.

He introduces the idea of “fourth spaces”—gatherings built around a shared purpose—and explains how the simple act of deciding why we're here and how we want to show up can fundamentally change the way we connect with others.

What if the simplest way to build a stronger team isn’t another meeting, leadership strategy, or team-building exercise—but sharing a meal?

Cody Hand shares a powerful lesson from a difficult chapter in his leadership career, when his team was fragmented, unhappy, and disconnected. Despite following traditional leadership practices, one of his strongest employees ultimately left because she felt lonely and excluded.

That experience led Cody to explore an ancient human instinct: we eat what we trust.

Inspired by the idea of communal dining, Cody began hosting weekly, scratch-made lunches for his team with two simple rules: no technology and no shop talk. What started as a meal became something much more meaningful—a space where people could slow down, find common ground, and build genuine relationships.

title: The secret to building trust is sitting at the same table | Cody Hand | TEDxThird Ward Salon
